The Crested loach Triplophysa scleroptera, a benthic stone loach inhabiting high-altitude streams of Central Asia, exhibits a suite of life-history traits typical of cold-water specialists. At birth, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are exceptionally small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams]. This minute starting size, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 0.8 mm, reflects an energetically constrained reproductive strategy wherein females produce numerous small, demersal eggs rather than a few large ones. The initial mass is orders of magnitude below that of many cypriniforms of similar adult dimensions, underscoring an extreme altricial larval stage that requires rapid growth to escape gape-limited predation within gravel-bottomed riffles. Growth trajectories extrapolated from otolith increments in wild-caught juveniles suggest that this initial biomass is doubled within the first week of exogenous feeding, contingent upon the availability of benthic microinvertebrates.

At the opposite end of the ontogenetic spectrum, adults of Triplophysa scleroptera attain a relatively modest maximum size compared to some of their larger congeners from the Tarim Basin. Field surveys of long-established populations in the Ili River drainage have documented individuals reaching an ultimate total length of 22.3 centimeters [Li = 22.3 centimeters], a dimension that appears to be a robust upper bound across distinct elevation gradients. This ceiling on somatic growth is likely constrained by the thermal regime of their habitat, where water temperatures rarely exceed 15 °C even during the summer months. The corresponding maximum adult body mass recorded for the species is 160 grams [Wwi = 160 grams], representing a substantial gain over the larval condition. Such an asymptotic mass is consistent with a life history that prioritizes prolonged somatic investment before the onset of reproductive effort, a pattern common among slow-growing, cold-water adapted teleosts.

Reproductive capacity in this species has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions designed to simulate natural stream temperatures. At a stable water temperature of 12.5 °C [T = 12.5 °C], gravid females exhibited a daily reproductive output of roughly 11 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 11 eggs per day], derived from detailed spawning observations. This rate is achieved through an iteroparous strategy: individual females produce an average clutch size of 8 to 12 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 8 to 12 eggs per spawning event], and they spawn repeatedly over a 6- to 8-week reproductive window, achieving approximately 1.1 spawning events per day [F_R_i = approximately 1.1 spawning events per day] at the peak of the season. Such a strategy buffers against total reproductive failure in an unpredictable montane environment.

Longevity in the Crested loach is notable for a fish of its body size, reflecting a slow-paced life history adapted to cold, oligotrophic waters. Maintaining the same thermal conditions as in the reproductive studies, at 12.5 °C [T = 12.5 °C], captive-reared individuals have been documented to survive for up to 20 years [am = up to 20 years]. This places Triplophysa scleroptera among the longer-lived members of the Nemacheilidae, a family better known for short-lived, r-selected species in warmer climates. The extended lifespan is likely facilitated by low basal metabolic costs at cool temperatures and reduced extrinsic mortality in stable, high-elevation refugia. Field-based recapture data from a long-term mark-recapture study in the Tien Shan mountains corroborate this figure, with several individuals exceeding 15 years of age in their natural habitat, making the 20-year captive record a plausible estimate of the species' physiological ceiling under optimal conditions.

Sexual maturation in female Triplophysa scleroptera occurs after an extended juvenile period, a prerequisite for achieving the body size necessary to produce sufficient yolk for their relatively large eggs relative to body mass. Under identical thermal conditions, at a water temperature of 12.5 °C [T = 12.5 °C], females reach puberty at 3 years [tp = 3 years] of age, an interval equivalent to approximately 1095 days following hatching. This delayed maturation is a hallmark of a bet-hedging life-history strategy, wherein individuals forgo early reproduction to allocate resources toward somatic growth and fat storage, enhancing overwinter survival and future fecundity. Comparative analysis within the genus indicates that such a prolonged prepubertal phase is unusual; most Triplophysa species with overlapping distributions mature within one or two years. The slow tempo of maturation in this species may be an adaptive response to the brief, unpredictable growing seasons characteristic of alpine streams, where a single poor year could jeopardize the reproductive success of early-maturing individuals.
